nameStory: Carpet bugle gets its name from its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit that forms dense carpets across the forest floor. The 'bugle' part comes from the shape of its small purple flowers, which resemble tiny military bugles or horns when viewed from the side.
description: Carpet bugle is a low-growing perennial groundcover that spreads by runners to form dense mats. This European native has dark green leaves with purplish highlights that stay close to the ground, growing only 2-3 inches tall. In spring, it sends up short flower spikes about 4-6 inches high, covered in small purple flowers that create a beautiful carpet of color across shaded areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small purple-blue flowers cluster densely on short upright spikes in spring, each flower shaped like a tiny bugle horn with an irregular opening

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Dark green oval leaves with purple-bronze highlights grow in low rosettes, feeling smooth and slightly thick to the touch with rounded teeth along the edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spreading mats by sending out runners (stolons) that root at nodes, creating an almost carpet-like groundcover

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems typical of the mint family, though you'll need to look closely at the flower stalks to feel the four-sided shape

habitat: Look for carpet bugle in partially shaded to shaded areas with moist, rich soil - woodland edges, under trees in parks and gardens, and along shaded pathways. It thrives in disturbed areas and has naturalized throughout New England, often escaping from gardens where it's planted as groundcover.

seasonality.spring: Purple flower spikes emerge in April and May, creating dense displays of color. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive bugle-shaped flowers are most visible.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade but the characteristic dark green leaves with purple highlights remain in low rosettes, still forming recognizable carpets.
seasonality.fall: Foliage may develop stronger purple tones as temperatures cool. The low-growing leaf rosettes persist and remain identifiable.
seasonality.winter: In milder winters, leaves may remain somewhat evergreen, though they become more subdued in color and may appear flattened against the ground.

funFact: Carpet bugle flowers are specially designed fly magnets - while most people think bees pollinate everything, this plant's unusual flower shape and color specifically attract hover flies and other dipterans rather than bees!
confusionNotes: The square stems and dense groundcover habit help distinguish it from violets, which have heart-shaped leaves and round stems. Remember: square stems and runners = carpet bugle, heart leaves and no runners = violets.
contextualKnowledge: Though it's in the mint family, carpet bugle doesn't have the strong aromatic scent typical of most mints when crushed. This European garden escape has become so common in New England that many people assume it's native.
compareHints: Carpet bugle differs from its relative blue bugle by its spreading runner habit - blue bugle grows in clumps without the characteristic carpet-forming stolons. If you see a dense mat spreading by runners, it's carpet bugle; if it's growing in individual clumps, it's likely blue bugle.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Blue Bugle differs from its much more common relative Carpet Bugle primarily in its growth habit - it forms tidy clumps rather than aggressive spreading mats.
